NC-2025-HB377.aiSummary: The bill would make a range of court changes, including in civil cases, court fees, records, and other court rules. It would clarify the difference between court costs and court expenses, and it would set fee amounts for use of court facilities in certain civil actions. It would also add a $20 fee for filing a notice of hearing on certain motions, with some exceptions, and it would take effect when it becomes law and apply to cases already pending or filed after that date.

NC-2025-HB308.aiSummary: The bill would make a range of criminal law changes in North Carolina. It includes rules on ignition interlock credit for people with out-of-state convictions, rights to information about sexual assault evidence kits, and changes to some crime penalties. It would also affect people and groups tied to metals recycling, pardons of innocence, and access to felony conviction records.

NC-2025-HJR1244.title: Adjournment Resolution.
NC-2025-HJR1244.policyArea: GENERAL ASSEMBLY; RATIFIED; RESOLUTIONS, JOINT; CHAPTERED; ADJOURNMENT
NC-2025-HJR1244.aiSummary: This resolution adjourns the North Carolina General Assembly’s 2025 regular session on July 2, 2026, and sets it to meet again on July 27, 2026, at 12:00 noon. It also limits what lawmakers may take up when they return, including budget bills, constitutional amendments, certain 2025 bills, local bills, appointments, veto overrides, election law bills, and other listed matters. It took effect when it was ratified.

NC-2025-SB602.aiSummary: The bill would let owners of certain downtown commercial buildings in Hurricane Helene disaster counties rebuild with the same fire-protection level for windows they had on September 27, 2024, instead of meeting newer state code rules. It applies only to eligible buildings being restored after Helene damage, and owners must file a notarized affidavit with the local building office. The exemption must be claimed within two years after the bill becomes law, and the bill would apply to buildings that get a certificate of occupancy on or after that date.

NC-2025-SB1047.aiSummary: The bill would rewrite North Carolina rules for guaranteed energy savings contracts used by government units. It would require public notice, a request for qualifications, reviews of bids, and an energy audit before a contract is signed, and it would add rules for how savings are checked each year. It would also make conforming wording changes in other state laws that refer to these contracts.

NC-2025-SB811.aiSummary: The act removes the cap on satellite annexations for Bailey, Weaverville, and Cherryville. It also removes listed land from the city limits of Morehead City and Washington, and from Kernersville, Red Oak, Vass, Waynesville, and Walnut Creek. NC-2025-SB558.policyArea: BOARDS; COLLEGES & UNIVERSITIES; COMMUNITY COLLEGES; COMMUNITY COLLEGES BOARD; DISCRIMINATION; EDUCATION; HIGHER EDUCATION; MINORITIES; PRESENTED; PUBLIC; RATIFIED; UNC; UNC BOARD OF GOVERNORS; VETOED; WOMEN; CHAPTERED; VETO OVERRIDDEN
NC-2025-SB558.aiSummary: The law sets rules for public colleges and universities in North Carolina, including UNC schools and community colleges, about diversity, equity, and inclusion programs. It bars them from promoting certain race- or sex-based ideas, using some DEI offices or staff, and requiring some courses tied to those ideas, with some speech and research limits left in place. Schools must also certify each year that they are following the law, and the first report had to include early steps and any spending cuts or job changes. The law took effect when it became law.

NC-2025-HR1239.aiSummary: This resolution honors the life and memory of James Michael Clampitt, a former North Carolina House member, and thanks him for his service to his community, state, and country. It also offers sympathy to his family. A copy of the resolution would be sent to his family, and it took effect when adopted.

NC-2025-HB171.aiSummary: The bill bans state agencies and local governments from using public money for diversity, equity, and inclusion programs or training, and from keeping DEI offices or staff. It also bars these bodies from using DEI in hiring, jobs, or contracts, and sets civil penalties and court actions for violations. The new state-agency rules take effect July 1, 2026, and apply to acts on or after that date.
